value_proposition: A full-stack quantum-computing platform centered on high-fidelity, fully connected trapped-ion hardware, fault-tolerance research, cloud and on-premises access, and integrated application and developer software.
target_customers: Enterprises pursuing chemistry and materials-science applications
computing_models: Hybrid quantum-classical computing using integrated NVIDIA GPU control resources
Streaming quantum computation through the disclosed gate-streaming feature
hardware_architecture: Quantum Charge-Coupled Device (QCCD) trapped-ion architecture with ion movement, all-to-all connectivity, mid-circuit measurement, and qubit reuse. Helios integrates NVIDIA Grace Hopper GPU resources into its control system.
physical_qubit_scale: Helios: 98 fully connected physical qubits. Physical-qubit counts for H1 and H2 are not supplied.
demonstrated_logical_qubits: Helios is presented as having 50 logical qubits. The supplied material does not specify the error-correcting code, physical-to-logical encoding, logical error rate, or workload conditions supporting this figure, so its relationship to fault-tolerant logical computation cannot be independently assessed from these sources.
two_qubit_fidelity: Helios: 99.921% average two-qubit gate fidelity, cited to Ransford et al. 2025. The website characterizes this as the highest average two-qubit gate fidelity among commercial quantum computers.
connectivity: All-to-all connectivity; Helios is described as having 98 fully connected qubits. Quantinuum says this eliminates swap gates required by fixed-connectivity architectures.
error_correction_strategy: Demonstrated capabilities are described as including real-time error correction, lattice surgery, break-even error rates, and beyond-break-even error rates. The architecture also supports mid-circuit measurement and qubit reuse, and all-to-all connectivity is positioned as enabling a wider selection of efficient or exotic error-correcting codes. Specific codes and Helios logical-error metrics are not supplied.
fault_tolerance_strategy: Scale high-fidelity QCCD trapped-ion systems while combining all-to-all connectivity, mid-circuit measurement, qubit reuse, real-time error correction, and software support. Large-scale, fully fault-tolerant quantum computing remains a future objective rather than a currently achieved capability.
roadmap: Current: commercially launched Helios with 98 physical qubits and a stated 50 logical qubits.
Long-term target: large-scale, fully fault-tolerant quantum computing.

BMW is expected to access Helios and successive planned generations, allowing progress to be validated at each stage; this does not establish that Sol or Apollo capabilities have already been achieved.
access_methods: Microsoft Azure access to Quantinuum Systems
InQuanto license for chemistry and materials workflows
ORNL Quantum Computing User Program credits for eligible U.S. researchers
manufacturing_strategy: The systems use Quantinuum's implementation of the QCCD architecture, and Helios is branded as powered by Honeywell. No fabrication partners, production volumes, supply-chain model, or detailed manufacturing strategy are disclosed.
software_stack: TKET quantum software toolkit and compiler
NVIDIA Grace Hopper integration in the Helios control system
developer_tools: TKET extension modules for devices and simulators
commercial_deployments: Multiple generations of QCCD-based Quantinuum systems are described as commercially deployed.
Helios is commercially launched and available through Quantinuum's cloud service and an on-premises offering.
System Model H1 is described as a commercial quantum computer.
BMW Group is using Quantinuum's trapped-ion systems for molecular and electrochemical simulation research and is to access Helios and future generations under a multi-year partnership.
More than 150 organizations are stated to be building on Nexus.
major_partnerships: BMW Group: multi-year collaboration in advanced materials, catalyst chemistry, electrochemistry, and sustainable mobility
JPMorganChase: financial analytics research and a Helios gate-streaming space-advantage project
Microsoft Azure: cloud access channel for Quantinuum Systems
ORNL: Quantum Computing User Program access for eligible U.S. researchers
NVIDIA: Grace Hopper GPU integrated into the Helios control system
Oracle: announced partnership to accelerate hybrid quantum-compute adoption on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure

BP and Synopsys: identified as customer-spotlight organizations
strengths: High disclosed physical-gate quality: 99.9975% one-qubit and 99.921% average two-qubit fidelity on Helios.
All-to-all connectivity can reduce circuit-routing overhead and avoid swap gates.
QCCD architecture provides flexible ion movement and supports mid-circuit measurement and qubit reuse.
The supplied material reports demonstrations of real-time error correction, lattice surgery, and beyond-break-even error rates.
Commercial access spans direct subscription, cloud, Microsoft Azure, Hardware-as-a-Service, and on-premises deployment.
Broad full-stack ecosystem covering programming, compilation, cloud orchestration, chemistry applications, and community support.
Sustained enterprise collaborations, including BMW since 2021, provide pathways for validating industrial use cases.
Helios combines quantum hardware with integrated NVIDIA GPU resources for hybrid control and computation.
weaknesses: Helios currently contains 98 physical qubits, while useful large-scale fault-tolerant computation remains a future goal.
The stated 50 logical-qubit figure lacks supporting details in the supplied material about encoding, code distance, logical fidelity, or error-corrected workloads.
No coherence measurements or gate-speed data are provided, limiting balanced comparisons against other modalities.
The sources provide component fidelity figures but not enough detailed logical-level performance data to evaluate sustained fault-tolerant computation.
Many highlighted applications are described as research, simulation, exploration, or potential capability rather than established production quantum advantage or quantified recurring customer value.
Comparative claims such as 'most powerful,' 'most accurate,' and 'only company who has solved the wiring problem' are not fully substantiated by comparative methodology in the supplied pages.
competitive_differentiators: Combination of high average two-qubit fidelity and all-to-all physical connectivity on a commercially accessible system
QCCD ion-transport architecture rather than fixed-location qubits
Mid-circuit measurement and qubit reuse for error-corrected and streaming workflows
Reported demonstrations of real-time error correction, lattice surgery, and beyond-break-even error rates
A stated 50 logical qubits on a 98-physical-qubit Helios system, although logical-qubit methodology is not disclosed here
Integrated full stack spanning Helios hardware, Nexus, Guppy, TKET, HUGR, and InQuanto
Cloud, Hardware-as-a-Service, and on-premises delivery models
NVIDIA Grace Hopper GPU integrated into the Helios control system
technical_risks: Maintaining current gate fidelity and all-to-all effective connectivity while scaling QCCD systems to substantially larger qubit counts may increase ion-transport, control, calibration, and system-integration complexity.
The disclosed logical-qubit count cannot be translated into fault-tolerant computational capacity without logical error rates, code details, and logical gate benchmarks.
Demonstrated error-correction milestones may not yet support long, commercially useful fault-tolerant algorithms at scale.
The absence of coherence and gate-speed disclosures prevents assessment of runtime limitations and the trade-off between high fidelity and execution speed.
Integrated real-time control, mid-circuit measurement, qubit reuse, ion transport, and GPU coordination create substantial hardware-software orchestration complexity.
Sol and Apollo require major scaling progress on fixed planned dates, creating execution risk even though the company states it has historically delivered systems on time and to specification.
commercialization_risks: Current customer examples emphasize collaborative research and exploratory value; broad evidence of production workloads with quantified economic advantage is not supplied.
Enterprise access appears oriented toward subscriptions, partnerships, grants, and sales engagement, which may limit frictionless adoption compared with fully self-service access.
On-premises deployment can introduce installation, support, service, and infrastructure complexity; commercial terms and deployment lead times are not disclosed.
The commercial proposition depends partly on planned Sol and Apollo systems arriving in 2027 and 2029 with meaningful performance improvements.
Claims of classical intractability, space advantage, and commercial value are not accompanied here by detailed customer ROI or repeatable production benchmarks.
Unspecified pricing, capacity, queue availability, service levels, and system production volumes make commercial scalability difficult to assess.
marketing_message: Quantinuum presents Helios as the most accurate commercial quantum computer and positions its high-fidelity, fully connected trapped-ion architecture and integrated software stack as a credible path from current enterprise experimentation to useful, large-scale fault-tolerant quantum computing.
messaging_gaps: The meaning and measurement methodology of Helios's 50 logical qubits are not explained.
No logical gate fidelity, logical error rate, code distance, or duration of logical operation is stated.
The phrase 'useful quantum computing' is not tied to a consistent quantified threshold for customer value or fault tolerance.
Claims of solving classically impossible problems are not accompanied on these pages by sufficient benchmark conditions for evaluation.
The assertion that Quantinuum is the only company to have solved the wiring problem is not technically defined or comparatively substantiated.
Roadmap descriptions do not provide target qubit counts, logical performance, fidelity, or application milestones for Sol and Apollo.
The relationship between Hardware-as-a-Service and the on-premises commercial offering is not clarified.
